transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Thank you for seeing me. Um, well, I guess I’m here because... things have just been really difficult in my head lately. I teach secondary school, and usually I can handle the stress of it, but lately, I just... I go to bed at night and I’ve started catching myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I didn’t wake up the next morning. Just, you know, if I just didn't have to face the day and it all just stopped. 

And then, on my commute—I have this long drive home from the school every afternoon, and the traffic is always so backed up, and I just sit in my car, gripping the steering wheel, and my mind just goes to these really dark places. I start wondering whether my family and my students would just be better off without me. Like maybe I’m just this burden and their lives would be so much easier and lighter if I just wasn't here anymore. And honestly, it really scares me. It terrifies me, actually, to have those thoughts playing on a loop in my own head, because I really don’t want to act on it. I don't. But they just keep creeping in, especially on that drive home when it's just me alone with my thoughts, and I just realized I couldn't keep ignoring it because it's incredibly frightening to have your brain telling you those things when you don't actually want to do anything to hurt yourself.
How long have you been experiencing these dark thoughts and feelings?

Um, let me think. It's been... well, it hasn't just been a few weeks, it's been quite a while, actually. I've been trying to pinpoint exactly when it started getting this bad, and I'd say it's been going on for about a year and seven months now. Yeah, a year and seven months. 

I know exactly when it started because it was right around the time the school district decided to completely overhaul our curriculum, and my principal asked me—well, 'asked' is a strong word, it was really more of an expectation—to take over the entire STEM assessment redesign. And, you know, I already had a full regular teaching load. I teach five periods a day, plus I have homeroom and grading, and suddenly I was supposed to be mapping out all these new rubrics and standardized testing metrics for the whole department on top of everything else. 

I just remember sitting at my dining room table late one night, probably around 2 a.m., just surrounded by all these binders and state standards documents, and that was the very first time I had that thought. That thought that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. Because the pressure was just so immense, and I felt like I couldn't breathe under the weight of it all. I kept telling myself, you know, "Just get through this semester, just get the pilot program off the ground and things will go back to normal." But they didn't. The redesign got finished, mostly, but those thoughts didn't go away. They just sort of settled in and became this constant background noise. So, yeah, it’s been a year and seven months of just... carrying this heavy, dark feeling every single day since I took on that extra project, and it just feels like this awful marathon I never signed up for.
Have you noticed any changes in your interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

Um, yeah, actually. That’s been another really hard part of all this. I used to be so active, you know? Like, I was always the person who had a full calendar and actually wanted to do the things on it. 

I’ve been part of this community softball league for years—we play every Tuesday evening in the spring and summer, and I used to look forward to it all week. I play second base, and it was just such a great way to blow off steam and laugh with other adults after dealing with teenagers all day. But lately... I don't know, I just stand there on the dirt and I feel absolutely nothing. I'm just going through the motions. Half the time now I end up texting the team captain that I have a migraine or I'm stuck at school grading, just so I can cancel and go home instead. 

And it's not just softball. It's everything. I have this neighborhood book club that meets on the last Thursday of the month, and I used to be the one who would actually read the whole book and bring the discussion questions and the wine, but now... I just skip it. I can't bring myself to go. And my garden... oh, my garden used to be my absolute sanctuary. I have these beautiful raised beds in my backyard where I grow heirloom tomatoes and peppers and zucchini, and I used to spend hours out there on the weekends, just getting my hands in the dirt. It was so grounding for me. But this past year, the weeds just completely took over. I’d look out the kitchen window at it and just feel completely apathetic. I just didn't care that it was dying. 

Even at school, I sponsor the robotics club, which used to be the absolute highlight of my week. Seeing the kids get so excited about their builds and competitions—it reminded me why I became a teacher in the first place. But now it just feels like one more heavy obligation I have to drag myself through. It's like the color has just been drained out of everything I used to love doing. None of it feels enjoyable anymore, no matter how hard I try to force myself to participate, so I just end up canceling on people and isolating myself, which I know probably isn't helping, but I just don't have the energy to pretend I'm having fun when I'm not.
Do you still find any pleasure in the things you do?

Um, honestly, like I was just saying with the softball and the gardening and all of that... no. Not really. I mean, I really try to find that spark, that actual feeling of pleasure, but it's just... missing. 

Like with the robotics club, for example. Just last week, the kids finally got this pneumatic arm working that they've been struggling with for a month. A couple of years ago, I would have been over the moon, you know? I would have been taking pictures for the school newsletter, high-fiving everyone, feeling that genuine warmth and excitement in my chest. But when it happened last week, I just stood there and gave them a fake smile. I was just going through the motions. I felt absolutely nothing. No joy, no pleasure, just... hollow. 

And it’s the exact same story with the book club and my garden. I keep trying to force myself to do these things, hoping the enjoyment will just magically come back if I fake it long enough, but it doesn't. I'll be standing there at second base during a softball game, or looking at my zucchini plants, and I just feel completely blank. So yeah, I just end up canceling most of my plans now because it's exhausting trying to pretend I'm having fun when none of it feels enjoyable in the slightest anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or the way you move throughout the day?

Um, yeah, I have. It's actually been really overwhelming. I just... I feel so tired all the time. But it's not just a normal tired, you know? It's not like the tired you feel after a long week or a bad night's sleep. It's this deep, heavy exhaustion that just sits in my bones. 

Like, take a normal Tuesday, for example. I get up, I go to school, I teach my five periods—which, you know, takes a lot of energy when you're dealing with teenagers and trying to keep them engaged with the material. And then usually I have a department meeting after school, or maybe I have to stay late to help a student with a project. And by the time I finally get home, my body just feels so incredibly heavy. It's like I'm wearing a lead suit. 

And the simplest things... things that shouldn't take any effort at all... they just feel impossible. Like, even just the thought of making dinner. I used to love cooking, I'd try new recipes and make these elaborate meals, but now? The idea of chopping vegetables or boiling water just feels like climbing a mountain. I can't do it. So I just end up eating cereal or toast, or sometimes I just skip dinner entirely because I'm too exhausted to even chew. 

And it's the same with work stuff, too. Like, answering a few parent emails. Usually, that's just a quick ten-minute task I'd do while watching TV in the evening. But now, I open my laptop and I stare at the screen, and my brain just feels like it's wading through molasses. Every single movement, every thought, it just takes so much effort. I feel like I'm dragging myself through the day, every single day, and I never actually get to rest. It's just this constant, heavy fatigue that never goes away, no matter how much I sleep.
Have you been having any problems with your sleep?

Um, yeah, actually. My sleep has been a total mess lately, which I'm sure isn't helping the exhaustion I was just talking about. It's so frustrating because, like I said, I feel this deep, heavy tiredness all day long, so you'd think the minute my head hits the pillow I'd just pass out, right? But that's not what happens at all. 

I'll get into bed, usually around 10 or 10:30, because I have to be up by 6:00 for school, and I'll just... lie there. I can be completely exhausted, physically drained, but my brain just won't shut off. I'll just lie awake staring at the ceiling, replaying every single thing I did wrong that day. Like, I'll obsess over an assessment deadline for my AP history class, wondering if I gave them enough time to prepare, or I'll replay a conversation with a student where I feel like I wasn't supportive enough, or I'll agonize over a mistake I made during a lecture. It's just this constant loop of anxiety and second-guessing myself, and it goes on for hours. 

And then, if I finally do manage to fall asleep, usually somewhere around 1 or 2 in the morning, it doesn't even last. I've been waking up almost every single night right around 4 a.m. Like clockwork. I'll just suddenly be wide awake, and my heart will be racing, and I'll look at the clock and see the red numbers glowing 4:03 or 4:12, and I just know it's over. I try so hard to go back to sleep. I'll try deep breathing, or I'll try counting backward from a hundred, or I'll try just lying perfectly still, but it never works. I never really get back to sleep. I just end up tossing and turning, watching the minutes tick by until my alarm goes off at 6:00, and then I have to drag myself out of bed and start the whole exhausting cycle all over again. It's just... it's torture, honestly.
Have you had any periods in the last year and seven months where you felt significantly better for a while?

Um, no. No, not at all. There hasn't been any break in it. It's just been this... this constant, heavy cloud hanging over me every single day. 

If I really sit and think about it, try to pinpoint exactly when this all started, it's been going on for about a year and seven months now. I know that sounds really specific, but I remember exactly when things shifted. It was right around the time I agreed to take over the STEM assessment redesign for the district. I don't know what I was thinking, honestly. I already had my full teaching load, the AP history classes, the robotics club, all the grading and parent emails... and then I just piled this massive district-level project right on top of it. 

I remember the first few weeks, I was trying to coordinate meetings with teachers from three different high schools, trying to align all these rubrics, and it was just... it was too much. And that's when I started feeling this way. At first, I thought I was just stressed, you know? Like anyone would be, taking on a huge project like that. I kept telling myself, "Just get through this semester, just get the first draft of the assessments done, and you'll feel better." But the semester ended, and the project kept going, and I didn't feel better. 

And then the next school year started, and I thought, "Okay, fresh start, new batch of kids, maybe this is when the fog lifts." But it didn't. It just stayed. Every single day for the last year and seven months, it's just been this exact same feeling of being completely drained and hollow. There hasn't been a single week, or even a weekend, where I woke up and felt like my old self. Not one. It's just been this relentless, unbroken stretch of... whatever this is, ever since I took on that assessment project. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, just a few days where I don't feel like I'm dragging myself through molasses, but it just hasn't happened. Not once in all this time.
Have you had to take any time off work or significantly reduce your work responsibilities due to the way you've been feeling?

Um, I haven't officially taken a leave of absence or asked administration to reduce my load, mostly because I wouldn't even know how to explain it to the principal without sounding like I'm just failing at my job. But... I *am* failing at it. Even though I'm physically showing up to the building every day, I'm just so incredibly far behind on everything, and it's definitely affecting my classroom. 

My lesson planning used to be so detailed, you know? I’d have these color-coded outlines, interactive activities, backup plans if a lecture ran short... but now? Now I'm literally just pulling up old slides from three years ago five minutes before the bell rings and just winging it, hoping the kids don't notice how disorganized I am. And the grading is even worse. I have stacks of essays from my AP history kids just sitting on my dining room table that I haven't touched in weeks. 

Actually, it's getting really bad. Just last week, I made this massive grading mistake that really, really scared me. I somehow entered the mid-term grades wrong for almost an entire period. I gave a student who earned a B- a D, and his parents immediately emailed the principal, and it was this whole big thing. It terrified me, honestly, because I used to be so meticulous. I was the teacher who double-checked every single rubric, who caught every little error, and I took pride in that. And now I'm just making these huge, sloppy mistakes because my brain just can't hold onto the information. 

And it's not just work, either. It's like my whole world has just shrunk down to this tiny, miserable little bubble. I've completely stopped showing up for my friends and my family the way I used to. My sister had a baby shower a couple of weekends ago, and I was supposed to be there early to help set up the balloon arch and the tables, and I just... I couldn't do it. I texted her that I had a migraine and I stayed in bed the entire weekend. I haven't seen my best friend for coffee in months, even though she keeps texting to check on me. I just leave her on read because even thinking of a reply feels like too much work. 

So, no, I haven't officially reduced my responsibilities on paper, but in reality? Most of my life has just narrowed down to barely, barely getting through the school day, surviving until the final bell, and then going straight home because I am just so utterly exhausted. There's just nothing left of me for anything or anyone else.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or the opposite, feeling restless and fidgety?

Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I know I just spent all that time talking about how incredibly exhausted I am, and how heavy and drained my body feels all day, but it's not like I'm actually moving in slow motion, if that makes sense? Like, if I need to hustle across the campus to the main office during my planning period to pick up a stack of scantrons, I still walk at my normal pace. I'm not physically moving slower than anyone else in the hallway. 

And my speech... no, I haven't noticed any changes there, and no one else has pointed anything out. I teach AP history, so I have to get through a massive amount of material in a forty-five-minute period, and I'm still talking at my usual speed. I still talk just as fast when I'm trying to cram in the last few details about the Industrial Revolution or explain the DBQ rubric right before the bell rings. The kids haven't looked at me weird or asked why I sound different, so I'm pretty sure my voice and my speaking pace are totally normal. 

And as for being restless or fidgety... no, definitely not. I mean, my brain is incredibly restless, like I said about lying awake at night overthinking every single thing I did wrong that day, but my body isn't. I'm not pacing around my classroom while the kids are testing, and I'm not tapping my foot or feeling like I need to jump out of my skin. Honestly, most of the time I just want to sit down and not move at all because I have absolutely zero energy. So, yeah, my mind won't stop spinning, but physically? I'm not bouncing off the walls with nervous energy or anything like that. I just sort of... sit there. So no, neither of those things really fit what's going on with me.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past year and seven months?

Um, yeah, actually. I have. It's funny you ask that, because just the other morning I was getting ready for work, putting on this pair of navy slacks that I used to wear all the time, and I had to pull my belt to the tightest notch just to keep them up. Over the past year, my clothes have just gotten noticeably looser, just hanging off of me. 

And the thing is, I am absolutely not trying to lose weight. I mean, I don't have the energy to even think about a diet or going to a gym right now. It's just... my eating habits have completely fallen apart. Most school days, I just completely forget to eat, or I honestly just avoid it. My lunch block rolls around at, like, 11:30, and the thought of walking down to the staff lounge, or even just opening a container of food at my desk, it just feels like way too much effort. I just sit there staring at my laptop, trying to catch up on all those emails and grading I mentioned earlier, and I just don't eat a single thing. 

I usually don't even realize I haven't eaten until late afternoon, like when I'm finally in my car driving home around four or four-thirty. And even then, it's not like I'm starving, it's just this empty, hollow feeling in my stomach. I used to be so good about it, too. I used to meal prep every Sunday, making these nice little salads and healthy lunches for the week, but now I don't even go to the grocery store if I can help it. So, yeah, I've definitely lost a noticeable amount of weight, but it's purely by accident because I just can't bring myself to eat during the day anymore.
Have you been feeling worthless or guilty about anything in particular over the past year and seven months?

Oh, God, yes. Honestly, the guilt is probably the loudest thing in my head most days. It’s just this constant, heavy weight sitting on my chest from the moment I wake up. Like I was saying earlier about how I’m just winging my classes and making those sloppy mistakes... whenever a lesson goes badly, which feels like almost every single day at this point, or even if just one student looks confused while I'm trying to explain a concept, I just... I completely spiral. 

Like, if I'm trying to get through a complicated lecture and I see a kid in the second row squinting at the board, clearly lost because my presentation is completely disorganized, I don't just think, "Oh, I need to clarify that for them." I take it as this absolute, undeniable proof that I am letting everyone down. I let that one confused look completely define me. And I can't let it go, either. I will go home and I just keep replaying that exact moment in my head, over and over and over again. I’ll be trying to make dinner or sitting in the living room, and my brain is just looping that failure. 

And then, of course, because I'm so distracted and drained by obsessing over how bad I am at my job, I end up checking out at home, which just adds another massive layer to the guilt. I just sit there replaying all my mistakes at work, and then I realize I'm ignoring my own child, and I just start telling myself that I’m a terrible teacher and a terrible mother. It’s like I’m failing the kids at school who rely on me to get them ready for their exams, and then I come home and I fail my own family because I’m just a shell of a person. So, yes, the feelings of worthlessness... they're pretty much eating me alive. I just constantly feel like I'm ruining everything I touch and letting absolutely everyone down.
Have you been having thoughts of death or dying repeatedly over the past year and seven months?

Um... well, yes. Actually, that's... that's a big part of why I'm here. It's really hard to admit, but... yes. Over the last year and a half or so, it's just been creeping in more and more. It's not like I'm sitting down and planning anything out, but I keep catching myself having these thoughts. Like, I'll be lying in bed, staring at the ceiling at 2 AM, feeling that crushing guilt I just told you about, and this thought will just pop into my head: "It would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up tomorrow." Just... if I could just go to sleep and that would be it. The alarm wouldn't go off, I wouldn't have to face the classroom, I wouldn't have to feel like a failure anymore. It just sounds so peaceful, you know? Just... stopping. 

And then, it happens in the car, too. I have about a thirty-minute commute, and sometimes I'm driving home after a particularly bad day—like when I've completely botched a lecture or when I'm just so exhausted I can barely keep my eyes open—and I find my mind wandering. I start looking at the oncoming traffic, or the concrete pillars under the overpass, and I catch myself wondering... would everyone just be better off? Like, really, truly better off without me dragging them down? I think about my students, how they deserve a teacher who is actually present and organized and not just barely surviving. And I think about my family, my husband and my child, and how they wouldn't have to deal with this empty, miserable version of me anymore. They could just move on and be happy. 

But then... then I snap out of it, and it terrifies me. It really scares me that my brain even goes there, because I don't *want* to act on it. I don't want to die, not really. I just want the pain and the exhaustion and the guilt to stop. But the fact that those thoughts keep happening, that they've been happening for so long now, and that they feel so rational in the moment... it scares me so much. That's why I finally made this appointment. Because I'm terrified of what happens if one day I don't snap out of it fast enough.
Have you experienced any periods where you heard voices or saw things that weren't there over the past year and seven months?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know my mind goes to some really dark places, like I was just saying, but I haven't ever... lost touch with reality, I guess you'd call it? I'm not hearing voices telling me to do things or seeing things that aren't there. It's just my own voice in my head, you know? Just my own thoughts running on that terrible, endless loop about how I'm failing everyone. 

Like, sometimes the house is completely quiet after my husband takes our kid out to the park just to give me a break, and I'll just be sitting there on the couch, staring at a stack of un-graded papers, and the silence is almost deafening. But it's just silence. There's no one whispering to me or anything like you see in the movies. It's just me, sitting there, feeling completely paralyzed by everything I have to do and everything I'm doing wrong. 

I do get startled easily these days, though. Like if I'm deep in one of those spirals of guilt and someone drops a book in the hallway at school, I might jump out of my skin. Or if the intercom buzzes unexpectedly in my classroom, my heart just starts pounding out of my chest. But I know it's just the intercom. I know it's just a book. I'm always fully aware of where I am and what's actually happening around me, even if I feel completely detached from it all. So, no, definitely no hallucinations or anything like that. Just... just my own brain being its own worst enemy, I suppose.
Have you felt like you're fidgeting or restless, or on the other hand, felt like you're moving slower than you usually do?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm restless or fidgety. I mean, I'm not pacing the halls or tapping my foot or anything like that. But moving slower? I'm not really sure about that, either. I don't think I'm physically moving in slow motion, like... like I'm walking through molasses or anything. I just... I don't know if I've really noticed a change in my actual physical speed. 

I mean, I know I mentioned earlier how completely exhausted I am all the time, and how it takes everything I have just to get out of bed and face the classroom. And sometimes it feels like a monumental effort just to stand up from my desk and walk over to the whiteboard. But I think that's more about the sheer lack of energy and the weight of everything I'm feeling, rather than me actually moving my body slower than normal. 

Like, when I'm trying to get dinner ready, which is a whole ordeal in itself lately, I don't feel like my hands are moving slower when I'm chopping vegetables or anything. I just feel incredibly drained while I'm doing it. And at school, when the bell rings, I still manage to get from my classroom to the staff room in the same amount of time, even if I feel like I'm dragging myself there. I haven't had anyone point out that I'm walking slower or talking slower, and I haven't noticed it myself. 

So, I guess... no? I don't think I've had either of those things. I'm not bouncing off the walls with nervous energy, and I don't think I'm physically sluggish in how I move. It's just the mental and emotional exhaustion that makes everything feel so incredibly hard to do. But the actual physical movements... I think they're pretty much the same as they've always been. I just haven't really noticed a difference in that specific way.
Have you felt like you're moving your body more than usual or been more active when you don't need to be?

No, not at all. If anything, it's kind of the exact opposite—though not in that slow-motion way I was just talking about, just in a... complete lack of extra movement kind of way, I guess? Like, I definitely don't have any sort of nervous energy or urge to move around when I don't have to. I know some people pace the floors when they're stressed, or they furiously clean the whole house, or they just can't sit still, but that is definitely not me right now. 

Before all this started, I actually used to be a pretty active teacher. I'd constantly be walking up and down the aisles, checking on my students' work, standing at the board, just naturally moving around the room while I talked. But now? Now I just sit at my desk at the front of the room for as much of the period as I can get away with. I don't even get up unless I absolutely have to. 

And it's the exact same way at home. Like, over the weekend, my husband was running around doing the laundry and vacuuming and trying to keep our kid entertained, and you'd think I would feel restless just sitting there watching him do everything. You'd think I'd jump up and start doing something, anything, just to be active or help out. But I just... sat there. Sunk into the sofa cushions. I don't fidget, I don't tap my fingers, I don't shake my leg. I just sit there feeling incredibly heavy. 

Sometimes I look at my students, especially the freshmen, and they're just bouncing their legs under their desks and tapping their pencils and shifting in their seats, and I just watch them and think, "Wow, what must it feel like to have that kind of excess energy?" Because for me, any extra movement just feels like a complete impossibility. I'm just trying to conserve whatever tiny, microscopic drop of energy I have left just to make it to the end of the day. So, no, definitely no extra moving around or being active. I don't even know where I'd find the fuel for that.
Have you felt like you're restless or have an inability to sit still?

No, no, I think... I think maybe I already answered that a little bit just now? But no, I definitely don't have any trouble sitting still. It's really the exact opposite. I mean, sitting still is practically all I do these days. 

Like I was saying about the weekend, just sitting on the couch while my husband does everything... I don't feel any urge to get up. I don't feel restless at all. There's no antsy feeling, no, you know, that feeling where you just have to stretch your legs or walk around the block because you've been cooped up too long? I don't get that anymore. It's like my body has just forgotten how to want to move. 

Even during staff meetings, which used to make me so antsy—you know how it is, sitting in those tiny library chairs for an hour listening to the principal drone on about standardized test scores—I used to be the one shifting around, checking my watch, crossing and uncrossing my legs, just dying to get back to my classroom and actually get things done. But now? Now I just sit there. I don't move a muscle. I just stare at the grain on the table and wait for it to be over. 

It's actually kind of strange when I think about it, how completely still I can be now. It's almost like I'm a statue sometimes. My husband asked me the other night if my legs were falling asleep because I hadn't moved from my spot on the sofa for three hours straight. And they weren't, I just... I just didn't have any reason or desire to move. The thought of getting up, of pacing, of being restless... it just feels so entirely foreign to how my body operates right now. So, no, absolutely no restlessness. I can sit still for hours and hours without even thinking about it.
Have you experienced any periods where your depression symptoms seemed to improve slightly, even if it was just for a short time?

No, not really. I mean, I wish I could say yes, I really do. I wish I could tell you that there was a day, or even just an afternoon, where the clouds kind of parted and I felt like myself again. But it's just been this constant, heavy, gray fog for... well, for weeks now. 

I keep waiting for it, you know? Like, I'll wake up on a Saturday morning, and the sun is shining, and I can hear my husband making pancakes downstairs, and I think, "Okay, maybe today is the day. Maybe today I won't feel like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight behind me." But then I try to sit up, and the exhaustion hits me, and that deep, hollow feeling in my chest is right there waiting for me, just like it was the night before. 

Even during things that used to make me so happy, there's no break in it. Like, last week, one of my students—this really sweet, quiet girl who has been struggling all semester—finally got a B on her history essay. She was so proud, and she came up to my desk to show me, and I smiled and told her great job, but inside... inside I just felt nothing. It was like I was watching it happen on a TV screen. Before, a moment like that would have buoyed me for the rest of the day, maybe even the rest of the week. But now, it doesn't even make a dent. 

It's just relentless. From the minute my alarm goes off at 6:00 AM to the minute I finally fall asleep at night, it's just the same flat, draining sadness. There are no good days, or even good hours. It doesn't matter if it's the weekend, or if we go out to a nice dinner, or if I'm just sitting on the couch doing absolutely nothing. The feeling is always there, exactly the same. I just... I haven't had any relief from it at all. It's like being stuck in a tunnel and you can't even see a speck of light at the end of it. So, no, definitely no periods where it feels like it's getting better, even for a little bit.
Have you had any difficulty concentrating on things like reading or watching TV over the past year and seven months?

Oh, absolutely. It’s actually been one of the most frustrating parts of all this, to be honest. You mentioned reading, and... well, reading for pleasure is completely out the window, but where it really, really impacts me is at work. Because, you know, as a teacher, reading and processing information is practically my entire job. But lately, my brain just... it just won't cooperate. 

I’ll sit down at my desk with a stack of assignments, and I’ll read the exact same student response three or four times. Literally, my eyes will track across the page, I’ll read every single word, but by the time I get to the end of the paragraph, my mind is just completely blank. I won't have retained a single thing. I’ll just sit there staring at the paper, and I still won't know what score to give it because the information just isn't processing. It’s like the words are just shapes on a page and they don't mean anything anymore. I used to be able to fly through grading, but now a handful of papers can take me all night because I just keep losing my focus or forgetting what I just read.

And it’s not just the reading, it’s the... the thinking part of it, too. The decision-making. My brain just feels like it’s wading through thick mud. Even the most basic, mundane tasks feel impossible to concentrate on. Like, just the other day, I had to put in an order for my classroom, and simple choices like which lab supplies to order can stall me for an hour. An entire hour! Just sitting there, staring at a catalog or a requisition form, completely unable to focus enough to just pick what we need and move on. It’s ridiculous. 

And TV is the exact same way. My husband will put on a show in the evening, something light, something we've even seen before, and fifteen minutes will go by and I'll realize I haven't absorbed a single piece of dialogue. I keep waiting for it, you know? Like, I'll wake up on a Saturday morning, and the sun is shining, and I can hear my husband making pancakes downstairs, and I think, "Okay, maybe today is the day. Maybe today I won't feel like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight behind me." But then I try to sit up, and the exhaustion hits me, and that deep, hollow feeling in my chest is right there waiting for me, just like it was the night before. 

Even during things that used to make me so happy, there's no break in it. Like, last week, one of my students—this really sweet, quiet girl who has been struggling all semester—finally got a B on her history essay. She was so proud, and she came up to my desk to show me, and I smiled and told her great job, but inside... inside I just felt nothing. It was like I was watching it happen on a TV screen. Before, a moment like that would have buoyed me for the rest of the day, maybe even the rest of the week. But now, it doesn't even make a dent. 

It's just relentless. From the minute my alarm goes off at 6:00 AM to the minute I finally fall asleep at night, it's just the same flat, draining sadness. There are no good days, or even good hours. It doesn't matter if it's the weekend, or if we go out to a nice dinner, or if I'm just sitting on the couch doing absolutely nothing. The feeling is always there, exactly the same. I just... I haven't had any relief from it at all. It's like being stuck in a tunnel and you can't even see a speck of light at the end of it. So, no, definitely no periods where it feels like it's getting better, even for a little bit.

Oh, absolutely. It’s actually been one of the most frustrating parts of all this, to be honest. You mentioned reading, and... well, reading for pleasure is completely out the window, but where it really, really impacts me is at work. Because, you know, as a teacher, reading and processing information is practically my entire job. But lately, my brain just... it just won't cooperate. 

I’ll sit down at my desk with a stack of assignments, and I’ll read the exact same student response three or four times. Literally, my eyes will track across the page, I’ll read every single word, but by the time I get to the end of the paragraph, my mind is just completely blank. I won't have retained a single thing. I’ll just sit there staring at the paper, and I still won't know what score to give it because the information just isn't processing. It’s like the words are just shapes on a page and they don't mean anything anymore. I used to be able to fly through grading, but now a handful of papers can take me all night because I just keep losing my focus or forgetting what I just read.

And it’s not just the reading, it’s the... the thinking part of it, too. The decision-making. My brain just feels like it’s wading through thick mud. Even the most basic, mundane tasks feel impossible to concentrate on. Like, just the other day, I had to put in an order for my classroom, and simple choices like which lab supplies to order can stall me for an hour. An entire hour! Just sitting there, staring at a catalog or a requisition form, completely unable to focus enough to just pick what we need and move on. It’s ridiculous. 

And TV is the exact same way. My husband will put on a show in the evening, something light, something we've even seen before, and fifteen minutes will go by and I'll realize I haven't absorbed a single piece of dialogue. He'll make a comment about what just happened on screen, and I just have to nod because I have no idea what's going on. I’m physically looking at the TV, but my mind is just... dial tone. It's exhausting, honestly. You don't realize how much you take your ability to just think clearly for granted until you suddenly can't do it anymore. I just sit there trying to force myself to concentrate, but nothing works.

Oh, well, it's been... gosh, it's been about a year and seven months now. I actually know the exact timeline because I can trace it right back to when things really started shifting at work. It was right when I took over the STEM assessment redesign for our department. 

You see, the district decided they needed to completely overhaul how we evaluate the science and math curriculum, and they wanted it aligned with all these new state standards. And for some reason, my principal thought I would be the perfect person to lead the initiative for our building. I didn't want to say no, because, you know, you want to be a team player, and I've always taken a lot of pride in my job. But the thing is, they didn't give me any course release time to do it. 

So I was suddenly expected to manage this massive, district-level overhaul, coordinate with all the other department heads, write up these endless rubrics and testing modules, all completely on top of my regular teaching load. I was still teaching my usual five sections, still dealing with all the daily lesson planning, the parent emails, the regular grading... and then I had this monumental task just dropped on my shoulders. 

I remember sitting in one of those initial planning meetings about a year and seven months ago, looking at the sheer scope of what they expected from us, and just feeling this incredibly heavy, suffocating weight settle over me. And that was really the start of it. That's when this whole cloud just kind of descended. I kept telling myself that once the initial rollout was done, I'd bounce back. I thought, you know, I just need to get through this semester, and then I'll be able to breathe again, I'll want to go out with my husband again, I'll enjoy my hobbies again. But the project just kept dragging on, the regular work kept piling up, and that low, empty feeling just... it just set in like concrete. It never lifted. So, yeah, it's been a solid year and seven months of just feeling completely hollowed out and detached from everything.
